title: Customer growth
description: How the customer base grew, where customers are, and who they are.

kpis.sql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', subscription_date) AS month, count(*) AS signups
  FROM customers
  WHERE subscription_date >= $since
  GROUP BY 1
),
t AS (
  SELECT count(*) AS customers, count(DISTINCT country) AS countries
  FROM customers
  WHERE subscription_date >= $since
)
SELECT t.customers,
       t.countries,
       (SELECT round(avg(signups)) FROM m) AS avg_monthly_signups,
       (SELECT strftime(month, '%B %Y') FROM m ORDER BY signups DESC, month LIMIT 1) AS peak_month,
       (SELECT max(signups) FROM m) AS peak_month_signups
FROM t

monthly.sql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT CAST(date_trunc('month', subscription_date) AS DATE) AS month, count(*) AS signups
  FROM customers
  WHERE subscription_date >= $since
  GROUP BY 1
),
x AS (SELECT month, signups, (month - DATE '2000-01-01') AS d FROM m)
SELECT month,
       signups,
       round(regr_intercept(signups, d) OVER () + regr_slope(signups, d) OVER () * d) AS trend
FROM x
ORDER BY month

top_countries.sql:
SELECT country,
       count(*) AS customers,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS share_pct,
       round(100.0 * sum(count(*)) OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC, country) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS cumulative_pct
FROM customers
WHERE subscription_date >= $since
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY customers DESC, country
LIMIT 15

weekday_month.sql:
SELECT month(subscription_date) AS month_num,
       strftime(subscription_date, '%b') AS month,
       isodow(subscription_date) AS dow_num,
       strftime(subscription_date, '%a') AS weekday,
       round(count(*) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT subscription_date), 1) AS avg_signups_per_day,
       count(*) AS signups
FROM customers
WHERE subscription_date >= $since
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4
ORDER BY 1, 3

email_tld.sql:
WITH t AS (
  SELECT split_part(split_part(email, '@', 2), '.', -1) AS tld, count(*) AS customers
  FROM customers
  WHERE subscription_date >= $since
  GROUP BY 1
),
r AS (SELECT tld, customers, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY customers DESC, tld) AS rk FROM t)
SELECT CASE WHEN rk <= 8 THEN tld ELSE 'Other' END AS tld,
       sum(customers) AS customers,
       min(CASE WHEN rk <= 8 THEN rk ELSE 9 END) AS slice_order
FROM r
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY slice_order

legal_form.sql:
SELECT CASE
         WHEN company LIKE '% LLC' THEN 'LLC'
         WHEN company LIKE '% Ltd' THEN 'Ltd'
         WHEN company LIKE '% PLC' THEN 'PLC'
         WHEN company LIKE '% Inc' THEN 'Inc'
         WHEN company LIKE '% and Sons' THEN 'and Sons'
         WHEN company LIKE '% Group' THEN 'Group'
         ELSE 'Other'
       END AS legal_form,
       count(*) AS customers
FROM customers
WHERE subscription_date >= $since
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY customers DESC

## Customer growth

A look at the 500,000-customer CRM sample: how many people signed up each
month, where they live, what their email addresses and company names look
like. Use the **Since** filter to restrict everything to sign-ups on or
after a date.

blocks.text:
### Data-quality note

**This data looks synthetic** (it resembles a Faker-style generated
customer file), for these reasons:

- **Flat sign-ups.** Every one of the 880 days from 2020-01-01 to
  2022-05-29 has sign-ups, at an almost constant ~570 a day. The
  month-to-month differences mostly reflect month length, not growth. The
  trend line is nearly flat, and so is the weekday by month heatmap.
  The peak month is simply a long month, not a real peak. The last month
  (May 2022) is cut off at the 29th.
- **Uniform categories.** Four of the five email TLDs (org, net, biz, info)
  hold ~10% each and .com holds 60%. The 243 "countries" (including
  Antarctica and Christmas Island) each get ~2,100 customers (about 0.43%);
  only Korea and Congo have double that, probably because the source
  country list has two entries for each.
- **Company names** follow three templates in equal thirds: "Surname Suffix"
  (LLC, Ltd, PLC, Inc, Group, "and Sons"), hyphenated surnames, and
  "A, B and C". The last two have no legal form, so they fall in *Other*
  (two thirds of customers).
- **Emails are unrelated to people.** Only about 0.3% of addresses contain the
  person's last name, and the email domain rarely matches the website.
  71 rows repeat an email address already used by another customer.

Treat the shape of this report as a demo of the tooling, not as business insight.
